newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Dangerous drivers should be banned EU-wide, MEPS say.
newsitem.headline: Dangerous drivers should be banned EU-wide, MEPS say.

text.p: Dangerous drivers who lose their licence in one EU member state should be banned from driving throughout the European Union, the European Parliament said on Thursday.
"We think it's a point of principle. If you're banned by one member state, that right to drive should be withdrawn throughout the Community," British Socialist Mark Watts told Reuters.

Watts was speaking after Euro-MPs had voted amendments to a European Commission proposal to harmonise the conditions under which motorists are authorised to drive, including minimum age and vision requirements, motoring skills and vehicle categories - COM(96)55.

The parliament agreed to the Commission's idea of a standard system for codifying the information which appears on driving licences, saying this would improve road safety and make free movement easier because it would make licences easier to check.
But Euro-MPs insisted the draft directive should increase motorists' obligations to match their increased rights to drive abroad.

They agreed amendments to oblige member states to extend mutual recognition of licences to cases of suspension or withdrawal and require the Commission to submit proposals for a European penalty-points driving licence system by March 31, 1997.
At present, motorists who commit offences in one EU country may continue to drive legally in the other 14.
If they commit an offence while in another member state, their licence is withdrawn for as long as they remain in that country but returned once they leave its territory.

If they are banned from driving in their home country, they can still apply for a licence in another member state, without necessarily having to inform that country's authorities of their earlier disqualification.
"These people are driving a dangerous weapon. We cannot afford to give them the benefit of the doubt," Watts insisted.
Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock told Euro-MPs on Wednesday the Commission supported EU-wide bans but did not have the power to propose changes to member states' widely different legal systems.
National officials had been discussing mutual recognition of driving penalties for eight years but legal and practical difficulties had blocked an agreement, a Commission official told Reuters.
Watts said Euro-MPs acknowledged there were obstacles but insisted that was no excuse for non-action.

Member states had agreed to an EU model of driving licence even though driving tests differed from one country to another, so they could act to reduce the numbers of deaths on Europe's roads, currently 50,000 a year, he said.
"Sadly, road safety takes a back seat in European politics," he said.
